title: Un appel de Rio  (A Call from Rio)

segments.t: This is the last scene of the episode. Cécile has refused the operation and asked Gabriel to be her agent again, so she stays with the agency, but the Tarantino film is gone. Back at the office, the agents sit down for their meeting with Andréa, Mathias, Gabriel and Arlette around the table, and Gabriel walks in looking very pleased with himself. Then a call comes through from Rio, where Samuel is on holiday. As usual, the French comes first; just listen, and we'll go through it together afterwards.
Gabriel, tu as l'air satisfait de toi.
On a perdu un gros contrat.
Mais on a gardé une grande actrice.
Mais on a perdu un gros contrat.
Un appel de Rio? C'est Samuel!
Samuel, on est en réunion. Tu es sur haut-parleur.
Ce n'est pas Samuel.
Bonjour. Je suis Jean-Louis d'Entremont.
Je vous appelle du consulat français à Rio.
J'ai de mauvaises nouvelles.
Monsieur Samuel Kerr est décédé.
Pardon? Quoi?
Il est mort à l'hôpital.
Il a avalé une guêpe.
C'est une plaisanterie?
Non, je suis désolé.
Let's walk through it gently. Gabriel arrives at the meeting, and Andréa notices his face straight away.
Gabriel, tu as l'air satisfait de toi.
'Gabriel, you look pleased with yourself.' The expression in the middle means 'to look' or 'to seem', and it is built on the verb 'to have'. Mathias is less happy.
On a perdu un gros contrat.
'We lost a big contract.' This is the everyday past tense: the helper verb 'to have', then the past form of 'to lose'. The small word at the start is the everyday 'we' again.
Mais on a gardé une grande actrice.
'But we kept a great actress.' The same past tense, with the verb 'to keep'. The adjectives for 'big' and 'great' both come before their nouns, which is normal for short, common adjectives.
Mais on a perdu un gros contrat.
'But we lost a big contract.' Mathias simply says it again. Neither of them wants to give up the last word.
Un appel de Rio? C'est Samuel!
'A call from Rio? It's Samuel!' The phone at reception rings, and everyone assumes it's the boss calling from his holiday.
Samuel, on est en réunion. Tu es sur haut-parleur.
'Samuel, we're in a meeting. You're on speaker.' Andréa talks to Samuel in the casual form, like one of the family. But the voice on the line belongs to someone else.
Ce n'est pas Samuel.
'It isn't Samuel.' Here the negation wraps around the verb 'to be'. The stranger introduces himself.
Je suis Jean-Louis d'Entremont.
'I'm Jean-Louis d'Entremont.' A formal way to give your full name to people you don't know.
Je vous appelle du consulat français à Rio.

'I'm calling you from the French consulate in Rio.' He uses the polite 'you', as an official should with strangers. Notice the shift: the agents speak casually to each other, but this man keeps his distance.
J'ai de mauvaises nouvelles.
'I have bad news.' The word for 'bad' is feminine and plural here, because news is a feminine plural word in French.
Monsieur Samuel Kerr est décédé.
'Mr Samuel Kerr has passed away.' This is the gentle, official verb for dying, the kind used on the phone or in a letter.
Pardon? Quoi?
'Sorry? What?' Andréa can't take it in. The first word is the polite one, the second is the blunt one.
Il est mort à l'hôpital.
'He died in hospital.' Unlike most verbs, the verb for dying uses 'to be' as its helper in the past, not 'to have'. Then comes the strangest detail.
Il a avalé une guêpe.
'He swallowed a wasp.' Back to the usual helper, 'to have', with the verb 'to swallow'. A sad and absurd end for the man who built the agency.
C'est une plaisanterie?
'Is this a joke?' A question made just by raising the voice at the end, with no extra words needed.
Non, je suis désolé.
'No, I'm sorry.' The word for 'sorry' here describes how he feels. And that is how the first episode ends. Let's hear the whole scene one last time.
Gabriel, tu as l'air satisfait de toi.
On a perdu un gros contrat.
Mais on a gardé une grande actrice.
Mais on a perdu un gros contrat.
Un appel de Rio? C'est Samuel!
Samuel, on est en réunion. Tu es sur haut-parleur.
Ce n'est pas Samuel.
Bonjour. Je suis Jean-Louis d'Entremont.
Je vous appelle du consulat français à Rio.
J'ai de mauvaises nouvelles.
Monsieur Samuel Kerr est décédé.
Pardon? Quoi?
Il est mort à l'hôpital.
Il a avalé une guêpe.
C'est une plaisanterie?
Non, je suis désolé.
That's the end of the first episode, and of a very long first day at the agency. Take a breath, be proud of how much French you've heard, and I'll see you in episode two.
Au revoir, Samuel.
